```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "100%", dpi = 96)
library(shadowscan)
f2 <- function(v) formatC(v, digits = 2, format = "f")
f3 <- function(v) formatC(v, digits = 3, format = "f")
big <- function(v) format(v, big.mark = ",")
ratio <- function(s, nm) s$ratio[s$candidate == nm]
# candidates that pass a screen, as words
lc_names <- c(fico = "FICO", dti = "DTI", amt = "amount", emp = "employment length",
              st = "state", pur = "purpose")
passing <- function(s) {
  p <- lc_names[s$candidate[s$verdict == "pass"]]
  if (length(p) == 0) "none" else if (length(p) == 1) p
  else paste(paste(p[-length(p)], collapse = ", "), "and", p[length(p)])
}
# Lending Club: small result objects shipped with the package
lc <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "lc2014.rds", package = "shadowscan"))
m <- lc$meta
# ACTG 175 is computed live and needs two suggested packages
ok <- requireNamespace("speff2trial", quietly = TRUE) &&
  requireNamespace("mgcv", quietly = TRUE)
# inline values are evaluated lazily, so they are skipped without the data
iv <- function(x) if (ok) x else "?"
```

The same question comes up wherever an outcome is missing for a reason that
may involve the outcome itself. This vignette takes two settings that differ
in almost every respect:

- **Reject inference.** Lending Club, 2014. A lender never learns whether a
  rejected applicant would have repaid, and it rejected them because it
  expected them not to.
- **Dropout in a clinical trial.** The AIDS Clinical Trials Group Study 175
  (Hammer et al., 1996). The CD4 count at week 96 is missing for patients
  who left the trial, plausibly those who did worse. In this literature the
  shadow variable is usually called a *nonresponse instrument*
  (Scharfstein, Rotnitzky and Robins, 1999; Zhao, Wang and Shao, 2021; Beppu
  and Morikawa, 2024; Chen and Shao, 2025).

Each step below is run on both, side by side. `vignette("shadowscan")`
explains the tools on simulated data.

```{r no-suggests, eval = !ok, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("**The ACTG 175 part needs the packages speff2trial and mgcv, which",
    "are not installed. Its code is shown but not run, its numbers appear as",
    "?, and the text describes the result obtained with the data.**")
```

## The data

**Lending Club.** The data have `r big(m$rows_all)` rows, and cross-fitting
the models takes `r round(m$crossfit_minutes)` minutes. The Lending Club
part therefore does not compute. It reads small result objects shipped with
the package. How to recompute them is shown at the end.

Lending Club published both its granted loans and the applications it
rejected. The two files share a few characteristics: FICO score,
debt-to-income ratio (DTI), amount, employment length, state and purpose.
For 2014 there are `r big(m$funded_all)` granted loans with a known outcome
and `r big(m$rejected_all)` rejections. $Y = 1$ is a default, and $R = 1$
means the loan was granted.

**ACTG 175** ships with the package speff2trial and is small enough to
compute here.

```{r actg-data, eval = ok}
data(ACTG175, package = "speff2trial")
d <- ACTG175
d$arms <- factor(d$arms, 0:3, c("ZDV", "ZDV+ddI", "ZDV+Zal", "ddI"))
d$y <- as.integer(d$cd496 < 200)
table(arm = d$arms, observed = d$r)
```

`r iv(nrow(d))` patients with HIV were randomised to four antiretroviral
regimens. The CD4 count at week 96 is missing for `r iv(sum(d$r == 0))`
patients (`r iv(round(100 * mean(d$r == 0)))`%). $Y = 1$ is a count below
200, the clinical threshold for AIDS. One caveat: for
`r iv(round(100 * mean(d$days[d$r == 0] < 672)))`% of the patients without a
week-96 count, follow-up ended before week 96. Some of them died, and for
them the count is not missing but undefined. The analysis follows the
literature and treats all of them as missing.

## The screen

### Lending Club: the coding matters

`shadow_screen()` takes each of the six characteristics in turn as candidate,
with the other five as covariates. With numeric characteristics entered
linearly:

```{r lc-screen-linear}
lc$screen_linear
```

Passing: `r passing(lc$screen_linear)`. But Lending Club cut hard. No
application with a FICO score below `r m$fico_cut` or a DTI of `r m$dti_cut`
or more was granted.
A linear term cannot represent such a step, so it understates how strongly
FICO and DTI drive the decision. Coded as ten classes of equal mass, the
picture changes:

```{r lc-screen-deciles}
lc$screen_deciles
```

Now only `r passing(lc$screen_deciles)` passes. Amount fails, with a ratio of
`r f2(ratio(lc$screen_deciles, "amt"))`. Amount has a further problem.
Loan amounts are heaped on round numbers, and many rows sit exactly on a
decile boundary, so classes cut at quantiles split those atoms arbitrarily.
`numeric = "classes"` cuts only between distinct values:

```{r lc-screen-classes}
lc$screen_classes
plot(lc$screen_classes)
```

Passing now: `r passing(lc$screen_classes)`. Amount has a ratio of
`r f2(ratio(lc$screen_classes, "amt"))`, DTI of
`r f2(ratio(lc$screen_classes, "dti"))`. The lesson is not that amount is a good shadow variable. It is
that the answer depends on the coding, and that a threshold rule in the
selection calls for classes.

### ACTG 175: a clear shadow variable and a clear violation

The covariates are baseline characteristics and the CD8 count at baseline.
The candidates are the CD4 counts at baseline (`cd40`) and at week 20
(`cd420`), sex, and `offtrt`, an indicator that the patient stopped the
assigned treatment before week 96.

Here the numeric characteristics enter linearly. Dropout follows no
threshold rule, and the screen finds no trace of one. Classes would also
cost more than the data carry: with `r iv(sum(d$y == 1, na.rm = TRUE))` counts below 200 among the observed,
ten classes for each numeric characteristic leave fewer than ten of them per
parameter, and the screen warns about exactly that. Flexible coding pays
when the selection uses a threshold and the sample carries the degrees of
freedom.

```{r actg-screen, eval = ok}
base <- c("age", "wtkg", "hemo", "homo", "drugs", "karnof", "race",
          "symptom", "str2", "preanti", "arms", "cd80")
sc <- shadow_screen(d, outcome = "y", response = "r", covariates = base,
                    candidates = c("cd40", "cd420", "gender", "offtrt"))
sc
plot(sc)
```

```{r actg-screen-numbers, include = FALSE, eval = ok}
v <- function(nm, col) sc[[col]][sc$candidate == nm]
```

- **The earlier CD4 counts pass clearly.** The count at week 20 predicts the
  count at week 96 far better than it predicts dropout, with a ratio of
  `r iv(f2(v("cd420", "ratio")))`.
- **Sex is too weak.** Its relevance has a $\chi^2/\mathrm{df}$ of
  `r iv(f2(v("gender", "relevance_chisq_df")))`. It has been used as an
  instrument in this literature, but on these data it carries almost no
  information about the outcome. Its point in the plot is hollow: its exclusion
  $\chi^2/\mathrm{df}$ is `r iv(format(signif(v("gender", "exclusion_chisq_df"), 2)))`,
  below the noise floor of 1, so its ratio divides by noise and is not
  reported.
- **Stopping treatment violates the exclusion restriction.** It is strongly
  relevant, but its ratio is `r iv(f2(v("offtrt", "ratio")))`: it predicts
  dropout more strongly still. It plays the part a bureau score plays in
  reject inference.

## The scan

### Lending Club: is the rejected portfolio riskier?

A lender asks whether its rejected applicants really are riskier than the
ones it granted. The decision threshold is therefore the default rate of the
granted loans, `r f3(m$threshold)`. It is itself an estimate and is treated
as fixed here. Rows with a FICO below `r m$fico_cut` or a DTI of
`r m$dti_cut` or more were never granted. There $r(x) = 0$, the data say nothing, and
these rows leave the analysis. That leaves the overlap region, `r m$overlap`,
with `r big(m$funded_overlap)` granted and `r big(m$rejected_overlap)`
rejected applications. Both models are logistic with natural splines for the
numeric characteristics, cross-fitted with `r m$folds` folds.

```{r lc-scan}
lc$scan_ci
plot(lc$scan_ci, ylab = "Default rate of the rejected")
```

```{r lc-numbers, include = FALSE}
s <- lc$scan_ci; lcv <- s$curve
fl <- exp(s$flip)
fp <- exp(lc$scan_plugin$flip[["sharp"]])
ft <- exp(lc$scan_ci_trim$flip)
```

Under MAR the rejected would default at a rate of `r f3(s$point)`. That is
above the threshold, but not by much. The estimated set reaches the
threshold at a propensity ratio of `r f2(fl[["sharp"]])`. That end of the set
is reached when applicants who would default were more likely to be granted
than otherwise identical applicants who would repay, as can happen when the
score misses what a loan officer sees. They need to be only about
`r round(100 * (fl[["sharp"]] - 1))`% more likely.

The confidence set is wider still. At $\lambda = 0$ it is
[`r f3(lcv$ci_lower[1])`, `r f3(lcv$ci_upper[1])`], which already contains
the threshold. Even under MAR the data cannot rule out that the rejected are
as good as the granted. This is with `r big(m$rows_overlap)` rows. Three
lines of the output explain why.

- **The rows with small $\hat r$.** `r big(s$tail[["target"]])` of the
  rejected rows have $\hat r < 0.01$. What the data say about them rests on
  the `r big(s$tail[["observed"]])` granted rows of the same kind, each
  weighted by $1/\hat r$.
- **The standard error.** The default `se_type = "max"` takes the larger of
  two standard errors at each endpoint. Here the empirical one is larger, by
  a factor of `r f2(lc$se$empirical[1] / lc$se$conditional[1])` at
  $\lambda = 0$. The conditional one is computed from the fitted models and
  misses their misspecification. The empirical one sees it, but it can be
  unstable where $\hat r$ is small. Taking the larger guards against both.
- **The plug-in.** Without debiasing, the scan on the same cross-fitted
  inputs flips at `r f2(fp)`.

Removing the rejected rows with $\hat r < 0.01$ changes the question to the
better-covered part of the rejected portfolio. For it the estimate flips at
`r f2(ft[["sharp"]])` and the confidence set at `r f2(ft[["ci"]])`:

```{r lc-trim}
lc$scan_ci_trim
```

### ACTG 175: every patient had a fair chance of being observed

Both models are logistic on the baseline covariates and the two earlier CD4
counts, cross-fitted with five folds. The rate of interest is the share with
CD4 below 200 among all patients.

```{r actg-inputs, eval = ok}
rhs <- paste(c(base, "cd40", "cd420"), collapse = " + ")
fe <- as.formula(paste("y ~", rhs))
fr <- as.formula(paste("r ~", rhs))
inp <- crossfit_inputs(d, "r",
  fit_eta = function(train, new)
    predict(glm(fe, binomial, data = train[train$r == 1, ]), new, type = "response"),
  fit_r = function(train, new)
    predict(glm(fr, binomial, data = train), new, type = "response"),
  folds = 5, seed = 175)
yb <- ifelse(d$r == 1, d$y, NA)
summary(inp$r)
all <- shadow_scan_ci(inp$eta_obs, inp$r, d$r, yb, target = "all")
all
plot(all, ylab = "Share with CD4 < 200, all patients")
```

```{r actg-numbers, include = FALSE, eval = ok}
acv <- all$curve; last <- nrow(acv)
```

The estimated chance of a week-96 count ranges from `r iv(f2(min(inp$r)))`
to `r iv(f2(max(inp$r)))`. This is the opposite of Lending Club, and it has
two consequences.

- **The sharp set is much narrower than the naive band.** At a propensity
  ratio of `r iv(f2(exp(acv$lambda[last])))` the naive band spans
  [`r iv(f3(acv$naive_lower[last]))`, `r iv(f3(acv$naive_upper[last]))`],
  the sharp set only [`r iv(f3(acv$lower[last]))`,
  `r iv(f3(acv$upper[last]))`]. Because every patient had a good chance of
  being observed, the observed share bounds what the missing ones can be.
  On Lending Club, where most rejected applicants had almost no chance of
  being granted, the two bands nearly coincide.
- **Sampling error is moderate.**
  `r iv(if (all$tail[["target"]] == 0) "No row has" else paste(all$tail[["target"]], "rows have"))`
  $\hat r < 0.01$, and the confidence set is only a little wider than the
  estimate.

## Comparing two groups

A trial is run for a comparison: is zidovudine alone worse than the
alternatives? `shadow_scan_contrast()` scans the difference in the share
with CD4 below 200 between two arms. It reports the selection strength from
which "no difference" can no longer be ruled out.

```{r actg-contrast, eval = ok}
others <- c("ZDV+ddI", "ZDV+Zal", "ddI")
k <- lapply(others, function(b)
  shadow_scan_contrast(inp$eta_obs, inp$r, d$r, yb,
                       target_a = d$arms == "ZDV", target_b = d$arms == b,
                       lambda = seq(0, 2, length.out = 201),
                       labels = c("ZDV", b)))
names(k) <- others
k[["ZDV+ddI"]]
plot(k[["ZDV+ddI"]])
data.frame(
  comparison = paste("ZDV -", others),
  mar = sapply(k, function(x) x$point),
  flip_estimate = sapply(k, function(x) exp(x$flip[["sharp"]])),
  flip_confidence = sapply(k, function(x) exp(x$flip[["ci"]])),
  row.names = NULL)
```

```{r actg-contrast-numbers, include = FALSE, eval = ok}
kd <- k[["ZDV+ddI"]]
```

Under MAR, the share below 200 is `r iv(round(100 * kd$point, 1))`
percentage points higher on zidovudine alone than on zidovudine with
didanosine. That finding holds as long as the propensity ratio stays below
`r iv(f2(exp(kd$flip[["sharp"]])))`. With sampling error it holds up to
`r iv(f2(exp(kd$flip[["ci"]])))`.

The end of the set that reaches zero is the least favourable case for the
finding. On zidovudine alone, patients who would end below 200 are that much
*more* likely to have their count taken, which makes the arm look worse than
it is. With didanosine added, they are that much *less* likely, which makes
that arm look better. Selection would have to run in opposite directions in
the two arms, and with that strength, to undo the comparison.

The same function compares any two groups chosen by $X$, such as two regions
of a lender. Each group is a whole segment of rows, observed and unobserved
alike. Comparing only the rejected applicants of two segments makes the
target depend on $R$, which the function does not cover.

## The mean of a continuous outcome

For the CD4 count itself rather than the share below 200,
`shadow_scan_mean_ci()` scans the mean count at week 96 over all patients,
with a debiased estimate and a confidence set. It needs, for every patient,
a grid of conditional quantiles of the count among the observed, fitted out
of fold. `crossfit_quantiles()` takes the learner as a function. Here it is a
location-scale model from mgcv for the square root of the count, smooth in
the two earlier CD4 counts, with the quantiles of its standardised residuals;
squaring the quantiles brings them back to counts. The response model is the
logistic regression from above.

```{r actg-mean, eval = ok}
loc <- as.formula(paste("sqrt(cd496) ~",
                        paste(c(base, "s(cd40)", "s(cd420)"), collapse = " + ")))
fit_q <- function(train, new, tau) {
  m <- mgcv::gam(list(loc, ~ s(cd420)), family = mgcv::gaulss(), data = train)
  p_tr <- predict(m, train, type = "response")
  p_new <- predict(m, new, type = "response")
  e <- (sqrt(train$cd496) - p_tr[, 1]) * p_tr[, 2]   # standardised residuals
  pmax(outer(p_new[, 1], rep(1, length(tau))) +
       outer(1 / p_new[, 2], quantile(e, tau, names = FALSE)), 0)^2
}
cq <- crossfit_quantiles(d, "r", fit_q,
  fit_r = function(train, new)
    predict(glm(fr, binomial, data = train), new, type = "response"),
  K = 200, seed = 175)
baseline <- mean(d$cd40)
km <- shadow_scan_mean_ci(cq$q, cq$r, d$r, d$cd496, threshold = baseline)
km
plot(km, ylab = "Mean CD4 count at week 96, all patients")
```

```{r actg-mean-numbers, include = FALSE, eval = ok}
i1 <- which.min(abs(km$curve$lambda - 1))
pl <- shadow_scan_mean(cq$q, cq$r, lambda = km$curve$lambda)
```

Under MAR the mean count at week 96 is `r iv(round(km$point))`, below the
mean at baseline of `r iv(round(baseline))`. The threshold is that baseline
mean: has the count fallen on average? The answer survives selection up to a
propensity ratio of `r iv(f2(exp(km$flip[["sharp"]])))` in the estimate and
`r iv(f2(exp(km$flip[["ci"]])))` in the confidence set. Beyond that, a
dropout that hides the patients with high counts could carry the mean back
to its starting level. At a ratio of $e^1$ the set is
[`r iv(round(km$curve$lower[i1]))`, `r iv(round(km$curve$upper[i1]))`]. The
plug-in, `shadow_scan_mean()` on the same inputs, gives
[`r iv(round(pl$curve$lower[i1]))`, `r iv(round(pl$curve$upper[i1]))`]. It
skips the correction terms, and here it
`r iv(if (pl$curve$lower[i1] >= km$curve$lower[i1] && pl$curve$upper[i1] <= km$curve$upper[i1]) "lies inside the debiased set, the direction of its bias" else "does not lie inside the debiased set")`.

## The two side by side

```{r side-by-side, eval = ok, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = c("Rows", "Observed", "Smallest r-hat, observed rows",
          "Rows of interest with r-hat < 0.01",
          "Finding", "Distance from the threshold at lambda = 0",
          "Flip of the estimate", "Flip of the confidence set"),
  `Lending Club 2014` = c(big(m$rows_overlap), big(m$funded_overlap),
                          formatC(s$tail[["min_r_observed"]], digits = 2),
                          big(s$tail[["target"]]),
                          "rejected riskier than granted",
                          f3(s$point - m$threshold),
                          f2(fl[["sharp"]]), f2(fl[["ci"]])),
  `ACTG 175` = c(big(nrow(d)), big(sum(d$r)), f2(min(inp$r[d$r == 1])),
                 big(all$tail[["target"]]),
                 "ZDV worse than ZDV+ddI", f3(kd$point - kd$threshold),
                 f2(exp(kd$flip[["sharp"]])), f2(exp(kd$flip[["ci"]]))),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrr")
```

Lending Club has about `r iv(round(m$rows_overlap / nrow(d), -1))` times as many rows, yet its finding is the
fragile one. Two things decide this, and neither is the number of rows.

- **How far the finding is from the threshold.** Under MAR the rejected
  lie `r f3(s$point - m$threshold)` above the threshold. The arms differ by
  `r iv(f3(kd$point))`. A small margin is crossed by weak selection. This
  drives the flip of the estimate.
- **How the selection treated the rows.** A lender that rejects most
  applicants is bound to leave rows that the data barely reach. Their
  weights $1/\hat r$ inflate the standard error, so on Lending Club the
  confidence set reaches the threshold already at MAR. A trial in which
  every patient had a fair chance of being measured does not have that
  problem.

## Recomputing the Lending Club objects

The source is the Kaggle dataset "All Lending Club loan data"
(wordsforthewise/lending-club, CC0 1.0), files
`accepted_2007_to_2018Q4.csv.gz` and `rejected_2007_to_2018Q4.csv.gz`. The
rejected file is restricted to 2014, and its `Risk_Score` column is used as
FICO. The code below outlines the computation. It is not run here.

```{r lc-recipe, eval = FALSE}
library(splines)
# d: one row per 2014 application, granted (R = 1, Y known) or rejected
# (R = 0), with fico, dti, amt, emp, st, pur.
vars <- c("fico", "dti", "amt", "emp", "st", "pur")
screen <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vars, function(z)
  as.data.frame(unclass(shadow_screen(d, "Y", "R", setdiff(vars, z), z,
                                      numeric = "classes")))))
ov <- d[d$fico >= 662 & d$dti < 40, ]
f <- ~ ns(fico, 4) + ns(dti, 4) + ns(log(amt), 4) + emp + st + pur
fit <- function(lhs) function(train, new)
  predict(glm(update(f, as.formula(paste(lhs, "~ ."))), binomial, data = train),
          new, type = "response")
inp <- crossfit_inputs(ov, "R", fit_eta = fit("Y"), fit_r = fit("R"),
                       folds = 5, seed = 2014)
ci <- shadow_scan_ci(inp$eta_obs, inp$r, ov$R, ov$Y,
                     lambda = seq(0, 2, length.out = 81), threshold = 0.1845)
```

The objects were built on `r m$built` with shadowscan `r m$package_version`.

## References

Beppu, K. and Morikawa, K. (2024). Verifiable identification condition for
nonignorable nonresponse data with categorical instrumental variables.
*Statistical Theory and Related Fields*, 8(1), 40–50.

Chen, J. and Shao, J. (2025). Instrument, variable and model selection with
nonignorable nonresponse. arXiv:2509.12557.

Hammer, S. M. et al. (1996). A trial comparing nucleoside monotherapy with
combination therapy in HIV-infected adults with CD4 cell counts from 200 to
500 per cubic millimeter. *New England Journal of Medicine*, 335,
1081–1090.

Scharfstein, D. O., Rotnitzky, A. and Robins, J. M. (1999). Adjusting for
nonignorable drop-out using semiparametric nonresponse models. *Journal of
the American Statistical Association*, 94, 1096–1120.

Zhao, P., Wang, L. and Shao, J. (2021). Sufficient dimension reduction and
instrument search for data with nonignorable nonresponse. *Bernoulli*, 27,
930–945.
